layers.about: Ethernet delivers a frame across the local link, using hardware addresses.

fields.label: Destination MAC
fields.what: Helps deliver this packet to a device or listening group on the local network, using its hardware address (MAC address).
fields.here: All zeros: no device address is supplied.

fields.label: Source MAC
fields.what: Gives the sending device's hardware address (MAC address) on this local network, so local replies can find it.
fields.here: All zeros: no device address is supplied.

fields.label: EtherType
fields.what: Tells the receiver which kind of packet is inside this Ethernet packet, such as IPv4 or ARP.
fields.here: 0x0800 selects IPv4.

layers.about: Internet Protocol version 4 addresses packets and lets routers forward them toward a destination.

fields.label: Version
fields.what: Tells the receiver which IP rules to use to read the packet.
fields.here: 4 selects IPv4 header rules.

fields.label: Header length
fields.what: Tells the receiver where the IPv4 header ends and the carried data begins.
fields.here: 20 bytes: the fixed 20-byte header plus 0 bytes of extra settings.

fields.label: Differentiated services code point
fields.what: Asks routers to give this packet a particular priority or handling policy.

fields.label: Explicit congestion notification
fields.what: Lets a router mark a packet when it is too busy, so the computers can slow down without losing that packet.
fields.here: This packet does not support a router marking it to report too much traffic.

fields.label: Total length
fields.what: Tells the receiver how many bytes belong to this IPv4 packet, including its header.
fields.here: 84 bytes belong to this IPv4 packet. The Ethernet or capture header is extra.

fields.label: Identification
fields.what: Helps the receiver join pieces of a split packet, called fragments, back together.

fields.label: Flags
fields.what: Controls whether routers may split this packet and whether more pieces follow.

children.label: Don't fragment
children.what: Tells routers to drop the packet if it is too large for the next link, instead of splitting it.
children.here: Set. A router must drop this packet if its next link needs smaller packets.
children.why: A rejection can reveal a path's size limit.

children.label: More fragments
children.what: Tells the receiver that more pieces of this split IPv4 packet follow.

fields.label: Fragment offset
fields.what: Tells the receiver where these data bytes fit in the original packet, measured in bytes.
fields.here: These data bytes start at the beginning of the original packet. This can be an unsplit packet or its first piece.

fields.label: Time to live
fields.what: Stops packets circling forever. Each router lowers this counter and drops the packet if it reaches zero.
fields.here: The counter is 64. Systems often start at 64, 128 or 255, so this packet has probably crossed no routers.
fields.why: A changed count from the same computer may suggest a route change. The starting count can also change.

fields.label: Protocol
fields.what: Tells the receiver what kind of data follows the IPv4 header, such as TCP or UDP.
fields.here: 1 tells the receiver to read ICMP next.

fields.label: Header checksum
fields.what: Helps detect damaged IPv4 header bytes using a calculated check number, called a checksum.
fields.here: 0x090a (correct). netmon checks the IPv4 header bytes, including this checksum, but not the carried data.
fields.why: An incorrect result suggests damaged header bytes or a checksum filled after capture. It does not check the carried data or prove who sent the packet.

fields.label: Source IP address
fields.what: Gives the IP address the packet claims to come from, so a reply can be sent back.
fields.here: 127.0.0.1 is loopback: traffic stays on this computer.
fields.why: The address alone does not authenticate the sender.

fields.label: Destination IP address
fields.what: Gives the IP address routers use to deliver this packet to its destination.
fields.here: 127.0.0.2 is loopback: traffic stays on this computer.

layers.about: Internet Control Message Protocol carries ping requests, replies and network error reports.

fields.label: Message type
fields.what: Tells the receiver what this network report is for, such as a ping or a delivery failure.
fields.here: 8 means echo request.

fields.label: Message code
fields.what: Gives the reason for a network report in more detail, such as which part of delivery failed.
fields.here: Zero is the required code for a ping request or reply.

fields.label: Checksum
fields.what: Helps detect damaged control-message bytes using a calculated check number, called a checksum.
fields.here: 0x6a71 is shown without verification. Only the IPv4 header checksum is checked here.

fields.label: Echo identifier
fields.what: Helps the ping program recognise replies to its own requests.

fields.label: Echo sequence
fields.what: Numbers ping requests so the program can match each reply to a request.

fields.what: Shows how many captured bytes netmon leaves uninterpreted because it does not decode their format.

children.label: FIN

children.why: The other direction can remain open.

fields.label: Window

fields.here: The receiver offers space for 65,495 data bytes. Opening packets always use the window without a multiplier.
fields.why: A zero window asks the other computer to pause sending ordinary data until space is available.

fields.why: A checksum can detect accidental damage, but it does not prove who sent the packet.

fields.label: Options

children.here: The sender can receive up to 65,495 TCP data bytes in one packet. IP and TCP header bytes are extra.
children.why: A smaller value can be normal on a path that needs smaller packets.

children.label: Selective acknowledgment permitted
children.what: Allows the other computer to report which data arrived beyond a gap, so missing bytes can be sent again.

children.label: No operation

children.label: Window scale

children.label: ECE

children.label: URG

children.label: PSH
children.what: Asks the receiver to pass the waiting data to its program without waiting for more data.

children.label: RST
children.what: Stops the connection immediately or refuses an attempted connection.

children.label: SYN

children.label: FIN

fields.label: Window

fields.label: Options
fields.what: Carries extra TCP settings or reports, such as a data size limit or which out-of-order bytes arrived.

children.label: Selective acknowledgment permitted

children.label: Timestamps

children.label: Timestamp echo

children.label: No operation

layers.about: Transmission Control Protocol provides an ordered byte stream. Sequence numbers and acknowledgments let the peers detect missing data.

fields.label: Sequence number
fields.what: Numbers data bytes so the receiver can put them in order and notice gaps. It gives the first data byte number, or the starting number when SYN is set.

fields.label: Acknowledgment number

fields.label: Data offset

fields.label: Flags
fields.what: Tells the other computer whether to open or close a connection, confirm receipt, or handle data specially.

children.label: CWR
children.what: Reports that the sender slowed down after a busy router was reported. During connection setup it helps agree to use congestion reports.

children.label: ECE
children.what: Reports that a router marked traffic as too busy. During connection setup it helps agree to use congestion reports.

children.label: URG
children.what: Marks the urgent pointer as valid, so the receiver can find the end of data needing special attention.

children.label: ACK
children.what: Marks the acknowledgment number as valid, so the other computer can see which bytes arrived.
children.here: Set. The acknowledgment number tells the other computer which byte is expected next.

children.label: PSH
children.what: Asks the receiver to pass the waiting data to its program without waiting for more data.

children.label: RST
children.what: Stops the connection immediately or refuses an attempted connection.
children.why: A reset does not by itself reveal why the connection fails.

children.label: SYN
children.what: Starts opening a connection by sharing the byte number from which this computer will count.

children.label: FIN

fields.label: Window

fields.label: Traffic class

fields.label: Flow label

fields.label: Payload length
fields.what: Tells the receiver how many bytes follow the fixed IPv6 header, including any extra headers.

fields.label: Next header
fields.what: Tells the receiver what to read next: an extra IPv6 header or data such as TCP or UDP.

fields.label: Hop limit
fields.what: Stops packets circling forever. Each router lowers this counter and drops the packet if it reaches zero.

layers.about: Transmission Control Protocol provides an ordered byte stream. Sequence numbers and acknowledgments let the peers detect missing data.

fields.label: Source port
fields.what: Identifies the sending program's port. The IP address finds the computer, and the port helps find the program on it.
fields.here: Port 18081 has no usual service listed in netmon. It may be chosen by the program or temporarily assigned by the operating system.

fields.label: Destination port
fields.what: Helps deliver data to the right program. The IP address finds the computer, and the port helps find the program on it.
fields.here: Port 57506 is in the range set aside for temporary or private use. The operating system often picks a temporary port for a client.

fields.label: Sequence number
fields.what: Numbers data bytes so the receiver can put them in order and notice gaps. It gives the first data byte number, or the starting number when SYN is set.
fields.here: The byte number is 3017068435. Comparing it with other packets helps locate gaps or repeated data.

fields.label: Acknowledgment number
fields.what: Returns a byte number to the other computer when ACK is set. In normal data exchange, it confirms earlier bytes arrived and names the next expected byte.
fields.here: 1887773310 is the next byte number expected from the other computer. The sender reports receipt of earlier bytes in this connection.

fields.label: Data offset
fields.what: Tells the receiver where the TCP header ends and the data begins, including any extra header settings.
fields.here: 32 bytes belong to the TCP header, including 12 bytes of extra settings.

fields.label: Flags
fields.what: Tells the other computer whether to open or close a connection, confirm receipt, or handle data specially.

children.label: CWR
children.what: Reports that the sender slowed down after a busy router was reported. During connection setup it helps agree to use congestion reports.

children.label: ECE
children.what: Reports that a router marked traffic as too busy. During connection setup it helps agree to use congestion reports.

children.label: URG
children.what: Marks the urgent pointer as valid, so the receiver can find the end of data needing special attention.

children.label: ACK
children.what: Marks the acknowledgment number as valid, so the other computer can see which bytes arrived.
children.here: Set. The acknowledgment number tells the other computer which byte is expected next.

children.label: PSH
children.what: Asks the receiver to pass the waiting data to its program without waiting for more data.

children.label: RST
children.what: Stops the connection immediately or refuses an attempted connection.
children.why: A reset does not by itself reveal why the connection fails.

children.label: SYN
children.what: Starts opening a connection by sharing the byte number from which this computer will count.

children.label: FIN

fields.label: Urgent pointer
fields.what: Locates the end of urgent data, meaning data needing special attention, when URG is set. It is an offset from this packet's sequence number.
fields.here: This pointer is ignored because URG is not set.

fields.here: Port 38328 has no usual service listed in netmon. It may be chosen by the program or temporarily assigned by the operating system.

fields.label: Destination port
fields.what: Helps deliver data to the right program. The IP address finds the computer, and the port helps find the program on it.
fields.here: Port 18443 has no usual service listed in netmon. It may be chosen by the program or temporarily assigned by the operating system.

fields.label: Sequence number
fields.what: Numbers data bytes so the receiver can put them in order and notice gaps. It gives the first data byte number, or the starting number when SYN is set.
fields.here: The starting number is 2609546217. SYN uses this number, so the first data byte starts at the next number.

fields.label: Acknowledgment number
fields.what: Returns a byte number to the other computer when ACK is set. In normal data exchange, it confirms earlier bytes arrived and names the next expected byte.
fields.here: 0 does not confirm receipt because ACK is not set.

fields.label: Data offset
fields.what: Tells the receiver where the TCP header ends and the data begins, including any extra header settings.
fields.here: 40 bytes belong to the TCP header, including 20 bytes of extra settings.

fields.label: Flags
fields.what: Tells the other computer whether to open or close a connection, confirm receipt, or handle data specially.

children.label: CWR
children.what: Reports that the sender slowed down after a busy router was reported. During connection setup it helps agree to use congestion reports.

children.label: ECE
children.what: Reports that a router marked traffic as too busy. During connection setup it helps agree to use congestion reports.

children.label: URG
children.what: Marks the urgent pointer as valid, so the receiver can find the end of data needing special attention.

children.label: ACK
children.what: Marks the acknowledgment number as valid, so the other computer can see which bytes arrived.

children.label: PSH
children.what: Asks the receiver to pass the waiting data to its program without waiting for more data.

children.label: RST
children.what: Stops the connection immediately or refuses an attempted connection.
children.why: A reset does not by itself reveal why the connection fails.

children.label: SYN
children.what: Starts opening a connection by sharing the byte number from which this computer will count.
children.here: Set. The sender proposes a starting byte number to open a connection.

children.label: FIN
children.what: Tells the other computer that the sender has finished sending data. It can still receive data.
children.why: The other direction can remain open.

fields.label: Window
fields.what: Tells the sender how much more data the receiver says it can take now. This keeps a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver.
fields.here: The receiver offers space for 65,495 data bytes. Opening packets always use the window without a multiplier.
fields.why: A zero window asks the other computer to pause sending ordinary data until space is available.

fields.label: Checksum
fields.what: Helps detect damaged TCP header or data bytes using a calculated check number, called a checksum. It also covers the IP addresses.
fields.here: 0xfe31 has not been checked by netmon. A network card may calculate it after capture, so an outgoing packet can appear to have a bad checksum.
fields.why: A checksum can detect accidental damage, but it does not prove who sent the packet.

fields.label: Urgent pointer
fields.what: Locates the end of urgent data, meaning data needing special attention, when URG is set. It is an offset from this packet's sequence number.
fields.here: This pointer is ignored because URG is not set.

fields.label: Options
fields.what: Carries extra TCP settings or reports, such as a data size limit or which out-of-order bytes arrived.

children.label: Maximum segment size
children.what: Tells the other computer the largest amount of TCP data this computer can receive in one packet, excluding IP and TCP headers.
children.here: The sender can receive up to 65,495 TCP data bytes in one packet. IP and TCP header bytes are extra.
children.why: A smaller value can be normal on a path that needs smaller packets.

children.label: Selective acknowledgment permitted
children.what: Allows the other computer to report which data arrived beyond a gap, so missing bytes can be sent again.

children.label: Timestamps
children.what: Helps measure how long a reply takes and distinguish old packets from current ones, using counters from both computers.

children.label: Timestamp value
children.what: Gives the sender's current timing counter so the other computer can echo it back.

children.label: Timestamp echo
children.what: Copies a timing counter received from the other computer so it can measure how long the exchange took.

children.label: No operation
children.what: Adds one padding byte so another TCP option can start at a convenient position.

children.label: Window scale
children.what: Offers a multiplier for later receive windows, so TCP can advertise space larger than its fixed window field allows.
children.here: Scale 10 offers a multiplier of 1,024 for later windows. It takes effect only if both computers offer scaling during setup.
children.why: Both computers must offer scaling during setup before it can be used. Opening packets always use the unscaled window.

fields.label: Payload size
fields.what: Shows how many data bytes the packet headers declare after the TCP header. A cut-short capture may contain fewer bytes.

info: Accepts the connection (SYN+ACK) — handshake 2 of 3, 13 µs after the request

fields.label: Version

fields.label: Header length
fields.what: Tells the receiver where the IPv4 header ends and the carried data begins.
fields.here: 20 bytes: the fixed 20-byte header plus 0 bytes of extra settings.

fields.label: Differentiated services code point
fields.what: Asks routers to give this packet a particular priority or handling policy.

fields.label: Explicit congestion notification

fields.here: This packet does not support a router marking it to report too much traffic.

fields.what: Tells the receiver how many bytes belong to this IPv4 packet, including its header.
fields.here: 52 bytes belong to this IPv4 packet. The Ethernet or capture header is extra.

fields.label: Identification
fields.what: Helps the receiver join pieces of a split packet, called fragments, back together.

fields.label: Flags
fields.what: Controls whether routers may split this packet and whether more pieces follow.

children.label: Don't fragment
children.what: Tells routers to drop the packet if it is too large for the next link, instead of splitting it.

children.label: More fragments

fields.label: Fragment offset
fields.what: Tells the receiver where these data bytes fit in the original packet, measured in bytes.

fields.label: Time to live
fields.what: Stops packets circling forever. Each router lowers this counter and drops the packet if it reaches zero.

fields.label: Protocol

fields.here: 127.0.0.1 is loopback: traffic stays on this computer.

layers.about: Transmission Control Protocol provides an ordered byte stream. Sequence numbers and acknowledgments let the peers detect missing data.

fields.what: Tells the receiver which IP rules to use to read the packet.
fields.here: 4 selects IPv4 header rules.

fields.label: Header length
fields.what: Tells the receiver where the IPv4 header ends and the carried data begins.
fields.here: 20 bytes: the fixed 20-byte header plus 0 bytes of extra settings.

fields.label: Differentiated services code point
fields.what: Asks routers to give this packet a particular priority or handling policy.

fields.label: Explicit congestion notification
fields.what: Lets a router mark a packet when it is too busy, so the computers can slow down without losing that packet.
fields.here: This packet does not support a router marking it to report too much traffic.

fields.label: Total length
fields.what: Tells the receiver how many bytes belong to this IPv4 packet, including its header.
fields.here: 52 bytes belong to this IPv4 packet. The Ethernet or capture header is extra.

fields.label: Identification
fields.what: Helps the receiver join pieces of a split packet, called fragments, back together.

fields.label: Flags
fields.what: Controls whether routers may split this packet and whether more pieces follow.

children.label: Don't fragment
children.what: Tells routers to drop the packet if it is too large for the next link, instead of splitting it.
children.here: Set. A router must drop this packet if its next link needs smaller packets.
children.why: A rejection can reveal a path's size limit.

children.label: More fragments
children.what: Tells the receiver that more pieces of this split IPv4 packet follow.

fields.label: Fragment offset
fields.what: Tells the receiver where these data bytes fit in the original packet, measured in bytes.
fields.here: These data bytes start at the beginning of the original packet. This can be an unsplit packet or its first piece.

fields.label: Time to live
fields.what: Stops packets circling forever. Each router lowers this counter and drops the packet if it reaches zero.
fields.here: The counter is 64. Systems often start at 64, 128 or 255, so this packet has probably crossed no routers.
fields.why: A changed count from the same computer may suggest a route change. The starting count can also change.

fields.label: Protocol
fields.what: Tells the receiver what kind of data follows the IPv4 header, such as TCP or UDP.
fields.here: 6 tells the receiver to read TCP next.

fields.label: Header checksum
fields.what: Helps detect damaged IPv4 header bytes using a calculated check number, called a checksum.
fields.here: 0xc2d9 (correct). netmon checks the IPv4 header bytes, including this checksum, but not the carried data.
fields.why: An incorrect result suggests damaged header bytes or a checksum filled after capture. It does not check the carried data or prove who sent the packet.

fields.label: Source IP address
fields.what: Gives the IP address the packet claims to come from, so a reply can be sent back.
fields.here: 127.0.0.1 is loopback: traffic stays on this computer.
fields.why: The address alone does not authenticate the sender.

fields.label: Destination IP address
fields.what: Gives the IP address routers use to deliver this packet to its destination.
fields.here: 127.0.0.2 is loopback: traffic stays on this computer.

layers.about: Transmission Control Protocol provides an ordered byte stream. Sequence numbers and acknowledgments let the peers detect missing data.

fields.label: Source port
fields.what: Identifies the sending program's port. The IP address finds the computer, and the port helps find the program on it.
fields.here: Port 38328 has no usual service listed in netmon. It may be chosen by the program or temporarily assigned by the operating system.

fields.label: Destination port
fields.what: Helps deliver data to the right program. The IP address finds the computer, and the port helps find the program on it.
fields.here: Port 18443 has no usual service listed in netmon. It may be chosen by the program or temporarily assigned by the operating system.

fields.label: Sequence number
fields.what: Numbers data bytes so the receiver can put them in order and notice gaps. It gives the first data byte number, or the starting number when SYN is set.
fields.here: The byte number is 2609547793. Comparing it with other packets helps locate gaps or repeated data.

fields.label: Acknowledgment number
fields.what: Returns a byte number to the other computer when ACK is set. In normal data exchange, it confirms earlier bytes arrived and names the next expected byte.
fields.here: 3081674313 is the next byte number expected from the other computer. The sender reports receipt of earlier bytes in this connection.

fields.label: Data offset
fields.what: Tells the receiver where the TCP header ends and the data begins, including any extra header settings.
fields.here: 32 bytes belong to the TCP header, including 12 bytes of extra settings.

fields.label: Flags
fields.what: Tells the other computer whether to open or close a connection, confirm receipt, or handle data specially.

children.label: CWR
children.what: Reports that the sender slowed down after a busy router was reported. During connection setup it helps agree to use congestion reports.

children.label: ECE
children.what: Reports that a router marked traffic as too busy. During connection setup it helps agree to use congestion reports.

children.label: URG
children.what: Marks the urgent pointer as valid, so the receiver can find the end of data needing special attention.

children.label: ACK
children.what: Marks the acknowledgment number as valid, so the other computer can see which bytes arrived.
children.here: Set. The acknowledgment number tells the other computer which byte is expected next.

children.label: PSH
children.what: Asks the receiver to pass the waiting data to its program without waiting for more data.

children.label: RST
children.what: Stops the connection immediately or refuses an attempted connection.
children.why: A reset does not by itself reveal why the connection fails.

children.label: SYN
children.what: Starts opening a connection by sharing the byte number from which this computer will count.

children.label: FIN
children.what: Tells the other computer that the sender has finished sending data. It can still receive data.
children.why: The other direction can remain open.

fields.label: Window
fields.what: Tells the sender how much more data the receiver says it can take now. This keeps a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver.
fields.here: The window field is 90. A multiplier may have been agreed during setup, so this packet alone cannot show the receive space in bytes.
fields.why: A zero window asks the other computer to pause sending ordinary data until space is available.

fields.label: Checksum
fields.what: Helps detect damaged TCP header or data bytes using a calculated check number, called a checksum. It also covers the IP addresses.
fields.here: 0xfe29 has not been checked by netmon. A network card may calculate it after capture, so an outgoing packet can appear to have a bad checksum.
fields.why: A checksum can detect accidental damage, but it does not prove who sent the packet.

fields.label: Urgent pointer
fields.what: Locates the end of urgent data, meaning data needing special attention, when URG is set. It is an offset from this packet's sequence number.
fields.here: This pointer is ignored because URG is not set.

fields.label: Options
fields.what: Carries extra TCP settings or reports, such as a data size limit or which out-of-order bytes arrived.

children.label: No operation
children.what: Adds one padding byte so another TCP option can start at a convenient position.

children.label: No operation
children.what: Adds one padding byte so another TCP option can start at a convenient position.

children.label: Timestamps
children.what: Helps measure how long a reply takes and distinguish old packets from current ones, using counters from both computers.

children.label: Timestamp value
children.what: Gives the sender's current timing counter so the other computer can echo it back.

children.label: Timestamp echo
children.what: Copies a timing counter received from the other computer so it can measure how long the exchange took.

fields.label: Payload size
fields.what: Shows how many data bytes the packet headers declare after the TCP header. A cut-short capture may contain fewer bytes.

info: Switches to encrypted mode (TLS Change Cipher Spec)

layers.about: Transport Layer Security negotiates encryption. Hello messages can be readable, but encrypted application contents are hidden.

fields.label: Record length

fields.label: Sequence number
fields.what: Numbers data bytes so the receiver can put them in order and notice gaps. It gives the first data byte number, or the starting number when SYN is set.
fields.here: This reset carries sequence number 0. Its meaning depends on the packet or connection being refused or stopped.

fields.label: Acknowledgment number
fields.what: Returns a byte number to the other computer when ACK is set. In normal data exchange, it confirms earlier bytes arrived and names the next expected byte.
fields.here: This reset carries acknowledgment number 2700148594. It identifies refused or aborted traffic, without promising that data was accepted.

fields.label: Data offset
fields.what: Tells the receiver where the TCP header ends and the data begins, including any extra header settings.
fields.here: 20 bytes belong to the TCP header, including 0 bytes of extra settings.

fields.label: Flags
fields.what: Tells the other computer whether to open or close a connection, confirm receipt, or handle data specially.

children.label: CWR
children.what: Reports that the sender slowed down after a busy router was reported. During connection setup it helps agree to use congestion reports.

children.label: ECE
children.what: Reports that a router marked traffic as too busy. During connection setup it helps agree to use congestion reports.

children.label: URG
children.what: Marks the urgent pointer as valid, so the receiver can find the end of data needing special attention.

children.label: ACK
children.what: Marks the acknowledgment number as valid, so the other computer can see which bytes arrived.
children.here: Set. The acknowledgment number is part of a connection refusal or abort.

children.label: PSH
children.what: Asks the receiver to pass the waiting data to its program without waiting for more data.

children.label: RST
children.what: Stops the connection immediately or refuses an attempted connection.
children.here: Set. The sender stops or refuses the connection.
children.why: A reset does not by itself reveal why the connection fails.

children.label: SYN
children.what: Starts opening a connection by sharing the byte number from which this computer will count.

children.label: FIN
children.what: Tells the other computer that the sender has finished sending data. It can still receive data.
children.why: The other direction can remain open.

fields.label: Window
fields.what: Tells the sender how much more data the receiver says it can take now. This keeps a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver.
fields.here: The window field is 0, but this reset stops or refuses the connection. Its window is not an offer to receive data.

fields.label: Checksum
fields.what: Helps detect damaged TCP header or data bytes using a calculated check number, called a checksum. It also covers the IP addresses.
fields.here: 0x128c has not been checked by netmon. A network card may calculate it after capture, so an outgoing packet can appear to have a bad checksum.
fields.why: A checksum can detect accidental damage, but it does not prove who sent the packet.

fields.label: Urgent pointer
fields.what: Locates the end of urgent data, meaning data needing special attention, when URG is set. It is an offset from this packet's sequence number.
fields.here: This pointer is ignored because URG is not set.

fields.label: Payload size
fields.what: Shows how many data bytes the packet headers declare after the TCP header. A cut-short capture may contain fewer bytes.

layers.about: Ethernet delivers a frame across the local link, using hardware addresses.

fields.label: Destination MAC
fields.what: Helps deliver this packet to a device or listening group on the local network, using its hardware address (MAC address).
fields.here: All zeros: no device address is supplied.

fields.label: Source MAC
fields.what: Gives the sending device's hardware address (MAC address) on this local network, so local replies can find it.
fields.here: All zeros: no device address is supplied.

fields.label: EtherType
fields.what: Tells the receiver which kind of packet is inside this Ethernet packet, such as IPv4 or ARP.
fields.here: 0x0800 selects IPv4.

layers.about: Internet Protocol version 4 addresses packets and lets routers forward them toward a destination.

fields.label: Version
fields.what: Tells the receiver which IP rules to use to read the packet.
fields.here: 4 selects IPv4 header rules.

fields.label: Header length
fields.what: Tells the receiver where the IPv4 header ends and the carried data begins.
fields.here: 20 bytes: the fixed 20-byte header plus 0 bytes of extra settings.

fields.label: Differentiated services code point
fields.what: Asks routers to give this packet a particular priority or handling policy.

fields.label: Explicit congestion notification
fields.what: Lets a router mark a packet when it is too busy, so the computers can slow down without losing that packet.
fields.here: This packet does not support a router marking it to report too much traffic.

fields.label: Total length
fields.what: Tells the receiver how many bytes belong to this IPv4 packet, including its header.
fields.here: 34 bytes belong to this IPv4 packet. The Ethernet or capture header is extra.

fields.label: Identification
fields.what: Helps the receiver join pieces of a split packet, called fragments, back together.

fields.label: Flags
fields.what: Controls whether routers may split this packet and whether more pieces follow.

children.label: Don't fragment
children.what: Tells routers to drop the packet if it is too large for the next link, instead of splitting it.
children.here: Set. A router must drop this packet if its next link needs smaller packets.
children.why: A rejection can reveal a path's size limit.

children.label: More fragments
children.what: Tells the receiver that more pieces of this split IPv4 packet follow.

fields.label: Fragment offset
fields.what: Tells the receiver where these data bytes fit in the original packet, measured in bytes.
fields.here: These data bytes start at the beginning of the original packet. This can be an unsplit packet or its first piece.

fields.label: Time to live
fields.what: Stops packets circling forever. Each router lowers this counter and drops the packet if it reaches zero.
fields.here: The counter is 64. Systems often start at 64, 128 or 255, so this packet has probably crossed no routers.
fields.why: A changed count from the same computer may suggest a route change. The starting count can also change.

fields.label: Protocol
fields.what: Tells the receiver what kind of data follows the IPv4 header, such as TCP or UDP.
fields.here: 17 tells the receiver to read UDP next.

fields.label: Header checksum
fields.what: Helps detect damaged IPv4 header bytes using a calculated check number, called a checksum.
fields.here: 0x5038 (correct). netmon checks the IPv4 header bytes, including this checksum, but not the carried data.
fields.why: An incorrect result suggests damaged header bytes or a checksum filled after capture. It does not check the carried data or prove who sent the packet.

fields.label: Source IP address
fields.what: Gives the IP address the packet claims to come from, so a reply can be sent back.
fields.here: 127.0.0.1 is loopback: traffic stays on this computer.
fields.why: The address alone does not authenticate the sender.

fields.label: Destination IP address
fields.what: Gives the IP address routers use to deliver this packet to its destination.
fields.here: 127.0.0.2 is loopback: traffic stays on this computer.

fields.label: Destination port

fields.here: Port 18998 has no usual service listed in netmon. It may be chosen by the program or temporarily assigned by the operating system.

fields.label: Length
fields.what: Tells the receiver how many bytes belong to this UDP packet, including its eight-byte header.
fields.here: 14 bytes: 8 header bytes and 6 payload bytes.

fields.label: Checksum

fields.here: 0xfe22 has not been checked by netmon. A network card may calculate it after capture, so an outgoing packet can appear to have a bad checksum.
fields.why: A checksum can detect accidental damage, but it does not prove who sent the packet.

fields.label: Payload size
fields.what: Shows how many data bytes the UDP header declares. A cut-short capture may contain fewer bytes.
